extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, philosophers of mathematics, mathematics students, and interested educated general readers
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and conceptual standards for judging accounts of mathematical knowledge, intuition, and reality (Platonism, formalism, constructivism), including how to develop mathematical intuition (e.g., four-dimensional) and how to situate mathematics in Popper's Worlds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop four-dimensional intuition via simulation and manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use computer systems to simulate handling, moving and seeing four-dimensional objects (e.g., hypercubes) so humans can develop four-dimensional intuition akin to 3-D intuition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design systems that permit real-time display and active manipulation (kinesthetic) as well as passive observation (visual). Empirically study adults (mathematically trained or naive) with objective psychological tests to document development of 4-D intuition and to distinguish visual vs. kinesthetic contributions. This reduces reliance on 'intuition' as an unanalyzed explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use 'intuition' as a catch-all explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid treating intuition as a blanket excuse for anything mysterious or problematical in mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead of invoking intuition vaguely, subject intuitive claims to empirical or methodological scrutiny (e.g., psychological testing, explicit constructive demonstration, or formal argument).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat mathematical truth as fallible and corrigible
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject the unspoken assumption that mathematics must be a source of indubitable truth; mathematical truth is like other truths: fallible and corrigible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophies and accounts of mathematics should accommodate historical and everyday evidence that mathematical knowledge can change, be corrected, or evolve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy should account for mathematics as tentative and evolving
rubrics_metrics.description: The task of mathematical philosophy is not to seek indubitable foundations but to give an account of mathematical knowledge as it really is—fallible, corrigible, tentative, and evolving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt explanatory frameworks that describe how mathematics is created, tested, accepted, and revised in practice rather than pursuing unattainable absolute certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept two empirical facts about mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Fact 1: Mathematics is a human invention (mathematicians create mathematical concepts). Fact 2: Mathematical objects have definite properties; there are true facts about them that we may discover or fail to discover.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any adequate philosophical account should reconcile both facts rather than accepting only one. Use these as starting constraints for evaluating philosophical positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconcile creation and objectivity of mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop a viewpoint broad enough to accept that mathematics is both created by humans and yet exhibits objective properties independent of any single mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid forcing a choice between Platonism (which privileges Fact 2) and formalism/constructivism (which privilege Fact 1). Seek frameworks (e.g., Lakatos, Popper) that can accommodate both the inventiveness and the discoverability aspects of mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Popper's World 1/2/3 framework to situate mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Locate mathematics in 'World 3'—the realm of social products: theories, language, traditions, and nonmaterial culture—distinct from World 1 (physical) and World 2 (individual consciousness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This framing supports the view that mathematics is objective (external to any one mind) but nonphysical and culturally situated. Use World 3 to explain how mathematical objects can be both human-created and have independent-seeming properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat mathematics as an objective ideal reality (neither subjective nor physical)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics constitutes an ideal (nonphysical) reality that is objective—external to the consciousness of any one person—but not part of the material world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical accounts should expand traditional categories (matter vs mind) to accommodate this kind of reality rather than forcing mathematics into existing inadequate dichotomies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize mathematics as a humanistic study with science-like qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics is intelligible within cultural shared understanding (like humanities) yet also achieves science-like consensus and reproducible, compelling results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating mathematical practice or claims, emphasize both the cultural, social, and humanistic aspects (meaning derived from shared understanding) and the standards that give mathematics its persuasive, reproducible character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value freedom of mathematical construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics' essence includes freedom to construct and to make assumptions (Cantor's idea); this constructive freedom is a legitimate feature to be recognized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation of mathematical methods or theories should accept creative construction as a key component, while still scrutinizing resultant claims by standards of coherence, consequence, and discoverability.

rubrics_metrics.name: When faced with contradictory facts, seek a viewpoint that renders them compatible
rubrics_metrics.description: If two undeniably true but contradictory facts arise, we should change our viewpoint to find a perspective from which they are not contradictory but compatible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This methodological principle directs evaluators to adjust or enlarge philosophical categories or frameworks rather than dismissing or forcing choice between facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand and evaluate major philosophical stances by what they accept/reject
rubrics_metrics.description: Formalism accepts Fact 1 (mathematics as human creation) and typically denies independent mathematical existence; Platonism accepts Fact 2 (mathematics has independent truths) and views mathematical reality as transcendent; constructivism insists nothing is true until constructively proved, rejecting nonconstructive acceptance of Fact 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these characterizations as diagnostic criteria when assessing a philosophical position's strengths and weaknesses relative to mathematical experience and practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge that 'imaginary' mathematical objects have definite properties and true facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Even objects that are 'imaginary' or 'created' have definite properties about which there are true facts (e.g., once a number is written down it already has properties such as primality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical and methodological accounts should allow for truth-conditions and discoverability for such objects, and not dismiss them as mere fiction without consequences.
